name: Battle of Tsushima

sides.name: Empire of Japan
sides.strength: 4 battleships, 27 cruisers, 21 destroyers, 37 torpedo boats; modern Vickers-built capital ships and well-drilled crews

sides.name: Russian Empire
sides.commander: Zinovy Rozhestvensky (2nd Pacific Squadron), Nikolai Nebogatov (3rd Pacific Squadron, surrendered)
sides.strength: 8 battleships, 8 cruisers, 9 destroyers, plus supply ships, after an 18,000-nautical-mile voyage from the Baltic via the Cape of Good Hope
sides.casualties: About 4,380 killed and 5,917 captured; 21 ships sunk including 7 battleships; only 3 ships reached Vladivostok

summary: Rozhestvensky's Baltic Fleet completed a seven-month voyage around the world to relieve Russian Pacific squadrons trapped at Port Arthur, only to find the port had fallen during the transit. Tōgō intercepted the Russians in the Tsushima Strait between Korea and Japan on the afternoon of the twenty-seventh of May. He executed a 180-degree turn-in-place (the "Tōgō Turn") under fire that crossed the Russian T and exposed each Russian battleship in succession to concentrated Japanese gunfire. By nightfall the Russian battle line was sinking. Destroyers and torpedo boats finished off survivors overnight. Nebogatov surrendered the remnant the next morning.
significance: Tsushima was the first decisive fleet engagement won by an Asian power against a European one in the modern era, and a result that reshaped global geopolitics for decades. The defeat triggered the Russian Revolution of 1905, ended Russian eastward expansion, and emboldened Japanese militarism through the 1930s. Operationally it pinned a generation of pre-dreadnought design lessons that fed straight into the all-big-gun HMS Dreadnought launched the following year, opening the naval arms race that led to World War One at sea.
